column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
Where does a democratic government get its authority from, and which values is democracy built on?
Name some early Indian institutions that show a ruler sharing decisions with others instead of deciding alone.
When was the Constitution adopted and when did it come into force, and how can it change with the times?
Who is the ultimate source of power in a democracy, and what right lets every adult citizen use it?
Why can nobody, however powerful, be punished or let off without a legal process, and what does that do for people's trust?
List the guaranteed rights in the Constitution's chapter on rights and say what a citizen can do if one is violated.
What would go wrong if the same body made, enforced and judged the laws, and how does the judiciary check the others?
How can ordinary citizens check on what a government is doing and ask it for information?
After an election, which party or group takes charge of the government, who sits on the other side, and what law governs the parties?
Why must a democratic government pay special care to the weaker sections of society, and which Article says so?
Why can a small country let citizens vote on major decisions directly, while a large one elects representatives to decide instead?
In which system does the head of the executive come from within the elected legislature and answer to it, and in which is the president elected separately?
What features of Indian elections show how they reach a huge and diverse population, including people who are unable to read?
Besides voting, in what ways can people take part in governance in their own village or town, and which special provisions protect tribal self-government?
How did the path to women's voting rights in India differ from [[Britain]] and the [[United States]], and what barrier remains even so?
What share of seats in local bodies does the Constitution reserve for women, and how have many states gone beyond it?
Why is the press often called a pillar of democracy, and what does it do for ordinary people's concerns?
Which groups outside government use democratic methods and how do they connect ordinary people with the State?
What everyday actions by citizens can harm a democracy, and which social problems still limit equal participation?
What happened to rights and the press during the Emergency, and how did the people respond once elections were held in 1977?
How can a student prepare to take an informed part in public life, and which school-age programmes build civic responsibility?
What does it mean to say a democracy is never finished, and what does each citizen contribute to it day to day?
